passage: Diwali evening, and the lights in Chachi's flat have just gone out. In the candle glow sits one steel bowl of kaju barfi for all six cousins. "Wait till I bring the plates," Chachi calls from the kitchen. Vishal, five, sees Sahil's hand slide toward the bowl. Quick as a squirrel, Vishal grabs four pieces and stuffs his pockets. Sahil grabs five. The littlest cousins grab too. When Chachi comes back with plates and a torch, the bowl is empty, and little Mishti is crying because she got none.

qa.q: What was in the steel bowl?
qa.a: Kaju barfi.

qa.q: Why did Vishal grab four pieces so fast?
qa.a: He was worried that if he waited, Sahil and the others would take it all, so he grabbed in a hurry.

qa.q: How could Chachi share the sweets next time?
qa.a: She could hand out the pieces herself, one each per round, so no child feels they must grab before it is gone.

qa.q: What is it like for little Mishti when the bowl comes back empty?
qa.a: Mishti feels sad and left out, crying because the quick grabbing left nothing for her.

grounding: Children with one shared bowl of sweets each grab fast for fear the others will take it, and the bowl is emptied.

passage: Last summer, in the hottest week of May, our school tank ran dry on a Friday. I know part of why. Every break I let the tap by the playground run over my wrists to cool down, sometimes for five whole minutes. I thought, it's only me, it's one tap. But Sahil did it too. And the Class 6 kids filled bottles just to throw water at each other. On Friday there was no water for drinking or for the toilets, and Sister sent us all home early. Nobody cheered. Sahil nudged me. "Maria, that was us." My ears went hot, because I remembered every one of my five-minute splashes. Now I turn the tap off after one splash.

qa.q: On which day did the school tank run dry?
qa.a: On a Friday.

qa.q: Why did Maria's ears go hot on Friday?
qa.a: Maria felt guilty and embarrassed, remembering all the five-minute splashes that helped empty the tank.

qa.q: What could the school try so the tank lasts through summer?
qa.a: It could show every class how the whole tank depends on each tap, and put up simple reminders to turn taps off after one splash.

qa.q: What would change if only Maria had left the tap running?
qa.a: The tank might have lasted, but because Sahil and the Class 6 kids thought the same way, everyone's small waste added up.

grounding: A child lets the shared school tap run, thinking one person does not matter, and the tank runs dry because everyone thought the same.

passage: Looking back at last term's geography project, I think I saw it before anyone said it. There were six of us. Pema made the map. Rajni wrote the report and stayed after school to print it. The rest of us, me included for the first week, sent "nice!!" in the group chat and nothing else. Nobody had a named job, so nobody had to do anything. On the Thursday before submission, Rajni snapped at Pema over a missing legend, and Pema cried in the library. They weren't angry at each other. They were exhausted, and angry at us. That week I finally helped glue the charts, and Rajni muttered, "At least one of you showed up, Dorjee bhai." I felt like a fraud. For the next project, I asked for a list with each person's name next to a task.

qa.q: Who made the map?
qa.a: Pema.

qa.q: Why did Dorjee feel like a fraud?
qa.a: Dorjee felt ashamed, having sent only "nice!!" for a week while Pema and Rajni carried the load, and then being thanked for gluing a few charts.

qa.q: What did Dorjee change for the next project, and why does it help?
qa.a: Dorjee asked for a list with each person's name next to a task, so everyone is accountable and the careful few don't carry it all.

qa.q: How did Pema and Rajni feel by the Thursday before submission?
qa.a: They were exhausted and angry at the rest of the group, which came out as snapping and crying.

grounding: A student sees classmates leave a group project to the same two careful members, who end up carrying the load and resenting it.

passage: At the ITI hostel in Hazaribagh, the monsoon had made everything damp, and the shared kitchen smelled worse each day. Ujjwal left his dal pot "to soak" on Monday. Ramesh left a frying pan on Tuesday; one pan, he thought, what difference does it make? By Thursday the sink was stacked up to the tap, ants marched along the shelf, and a cockroach sat on the gas stove as if it paid rent. Six boys stood at the kitchen door. Each had left just one thing. Nobody could cook. That night they all ate dry biscuits in their rooms, and Ujjwal, hungry and annoyed, finally scrubbed his pot and then, grumbling, Ramesh's pan too.

qa.q: On which day did Ujjwal leave his dal pot?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling as he scrubbed the pots that night?
qa.a: He felt hungry, annoyed and a little guilty, knowing his soaking pot had helped start the mess he now had to clean.

qa.q: What small step would stop the kitchen piling up again?
qa.a: The six could agree that everyone washes their own pot the same day, and take turns checking the sink each night.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see his one frying pan?
qa.a: He thinks one pan makes no difference, not seeing that everyone leaving just one thing is what stacked the sink to the tap.

grounding: Hostel mates each leave one dirty pot in the shared kitchen, assuming it is too small to matter, until nobody can cook.

subtype: Setting rules everyone can live with [Response]
passage:
Tuesday.
The shared washing machine on our floor broke AGAIN. Third time this year. Someone keeps stuffing it with rugs.
Tonight I knocked on all four doors and asked for a ten-minute meeting on the landing. Tanuja from 3B came with a cup of tea; the old uncle from 3D brought a stool.
I'd drawn a chart: each flat gets two fixed evening slots, no rugs or blankets (the laundry shop for those), and whoever uses it last wipes the filter and signs the sheet taped to the lid. Skip the filter twice and you chip in for the next repair. Everyone nodded, even the rug person, I think.
Then I put my own name in the first slot and cleaned the filter in front of them. Disgusting.
Aadhya, building committee of one

qa.q: What did the old uncle from 3D bring?
qa.a: A stool.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel about the machine breaking again?
qa.a: Aadhya felt frustrated and fed up, since it was the third time this year, and that pushed Aadhya to call a meeting.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Aadhya to clean the filter in front of everyone?
qa.a: It made the rule fair and visible, so the neighbours could trust they were not being asked to do anything the organiser wouldn't.

qa.q: What might the rug person feel during the meeting?
qa.a: They may feel a bit guilty or caught out, but the fair chart lets them change without being shamed in public.

grounding: A young adult proposes a fair rota, clear limits and shared checking for a common washing machine, and follows the rule first.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
subtype: Share or cheat in a game [Actor]
passage: Sankranti holidays in the kasba meant kites on every roof and marble games in the lane behind the flour mill. Vaibhav and Noor had a deal: at the count of three, each would drop five marbles into the other's hand, no peeking. Vaibhav's fist held four good ones and one cracked one. He thought about slipping in two cracked ones instead. Last week the Pandey boys had cheated him in a swap, and he had felt so stupid. What if Noor did the same? One. Two. His palm grew sweaty. Three. Noor's five marbles clinked into his hand, all shiny, even the blue one with the gold swirl. Vaibhav looked at his cracked marble in Noor's palm and felt his face go hot.

qa.q: How many marbles was each child to drop?
qa.a: Five marbles.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav think about slipping in more cracked marbles?
qa.a: He was afraid of being cheated and feeling stupid again, as with the Pandey boys, so he worried Noor would cheat first.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav do now to keep the deal fair?
qa.a: He could admit the cracked marble, swap in a good one, and thank Noor for playing straight.

qa.q: How might Noor feel on seeing the cracked marble?
qa.a: Noor might feel a little let down after giving the best marbles, and wonder whether to trust Vaibhav next time.

grounding: A child in a marble swap is tempted to cheat because he fears being cheated first, while his friend plays fair.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage:
Subject: about the Chapchar Kut presentation mess
Hi Lalremsiami,
I've been thinking about Monday, and writing felt easier than saying it in class.
Honestly, I didn't do my half of the slides. You're so organised that I figured you'd fill the gaps like always. Then in the corridor you told me you'd skipped your part because you thought I'd finish it, since I'm "the one who likes speaking".
So we stood up with four slides and a lot of "umm". Mr Zothan gave us 9 out of 25. If either of us had just done our share, we'd both have been fine.
Can we redo it properly for the practical exam? I'll take the history and the pictures. You take the dance section?
Sorry, really.
Kamal

qa.q: What mark did Mr Zothan give the presentation?
qa.a: 9 out of 25.

qa.q: How does Kamal seem to feel while writing the email?
qa.a: Kamal feels embarrassed and sorry, finding it easier to write than to speak in class and apologising at the end.

qa.q: What does Kamal propose, and why is it a better plan?
qa.a: To redo it with clear halves, history and pictures for Kamal and the dance section for Lalremsiami, so neither relies on the other to cover.

qa.q: Why might Lalremsiami have skipped a share of the slides too?
qa.a: Lalremsiami expected Kamal to finish it, as the one who likes speaking, so each chose what seemed easiest and both ended up worse off.

grounding: Two teenagers each skip their part of a joint presentation expecting the other to cover, and both do worse than if they had cooperated.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: At the Bareilly college, winter exams came with fog so thick the rickshaws crawled. All semester Imran had photocopied his neat chemistry notes for anyone who asked, especially Aditi, who asked every week and never once shared hers. When the results went up on the notice board, Aditi was first. Imran was fourth. In the canteen he heard her tell someone, "I just used Imran's notes, he writes everything down." His neck burned. That night he told his roommate he was done: no more notes for anyone, ever. The next week Danish, a quiet boy who had once lent him a calculator, asked to study together for physics. Imran almost said no. He stood in the fog-wet corridor, deciding.

qa.q: What rank did Imran get?
qa.a: Fourth.

qa.q: How did Imran feel when he heard Aditi in the canteen?
qa.a: He felt foolish and angry, his neck burning, because his generosity had been used to beat him.

qa.q: What would you advise Imran about Danish's request?
qa.a: To judge Danish on his own record, like the lent calculator, and share with people who share back instead of shutting everyone out.

qa.q: How might Danish feel if Imran refuses?
qa.a: Danish might feel confused and rejected for something Aditi did, and Imran would lose a fair study partner.

grounding: A student whose freely shared notes helped a non-sharing peer rank higher feels foolish and angry and is tempted to distrust everyone.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
subtype: Cooperation that grows over repeated rounds [Actor]
passage: Three days before Eid, the tailoring shop in Bhopal's old market had forty orders and one working fan. Rehana and Seema, both twenty, had sat at neighbouring machines since they were seventeen. They had a system: whoever finished first took the other's hemming. Last year, during the wedding rush, a girl called Nazma had promised to cover Rehana's shift and then vanished; Rehana still didn't pass work to Nazma. At seven, Seema's mother phoned: Seema's little brother had a fever. Seema looked at her pile of twelve kurtas. "Go," Rehana said. "I'll hem yours. Tomorrow you do my buttons." The power went at nine. Rehana finished by candle and phone light. The next morning Seema arrived at six and did every button without being asked.

qa.q: How many orders did the shop have three days before Eid?
qa.a: Forty orders.

qa.q: Why did Rehana tell Seema to go and offer to hem her kurtas?
qa.a: She felt loyal and trusting, knowing from three years side by side that Seema would return the favour, unlike Nazma.

qa.q: Why is keeping promises the practical choice for Rehana and Seema?
qa.a: Because they meet at the same machines every day, each kept promise builds trust that helps them in every rush, while one betrayal is remembered, as with Nazma.

qa.q: How does Nazma's broken promise still affect her at the shop?
qa.a: Rehana still doesn't pass work to Nazma, so one broken promise has cost her trust long after the wedding rush.

grounding: Two young tailors who have worked side by side for years keep cooperating in the Eid rush, knowing reliability pays and a betrayal is remembered.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: In the Gurugram office, Imran's analytics team and Uday's sales team had to share one client dashboard. In week one, Imran sent Uday his cleaned data without being asked. Uday thanked him and sent back the client's feedback. Good. In week three, on the client call, Uday presented Imran's churn chart as "our sales insight". Imran didn't fume in the group chat or quietly stop sending data. After the call he walked to Uday's desk. "That chart was ours. Next time, credit my team, or I'll say it on the call." Uday went red. The next morning he emailed the client: "Correction: the churn analysis came from Imran's team." Imran messaged Uday privately: "Thanks. Friday's data is coming as usual." And it did.

qa.q: What did Uday present as "our sales insight"?
qa.a: Imran's churn chart.

qa.q: How did Imran feel about Uday's correction email?
qa.a: He felt relieved and respected, and was ready to trust Uday again, so he thanked him and kept sending data 🙂.

qa.q: Which of Imran's choices kept the partnership working?
qa.a: He shared first, called out the stolen credit plainly and in private, and forgave once Uday corrected it, avoiding both being used and a long feud.

qa.q: What is it like for Uday when Imran comes to his desk?
qa.a: It is embarrassing, and Uday goes red, but the plain warning gives him a clear chance to fix it without a public fight.

grounding: A young professional cooperates first, calls out stolen credit plainly and forgives once it is corrected.
